items.followUp: Define isotopes and name the three isotopes of oxygen, giving their mass numbers.

rubric.why: Identifies the shared atomic number and differing mass numbers that define isotopes.
rubric.how: Award for stating that isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

rubric.why: Names or symbolises all three isotopes of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award for naming or correctly symbolising protium, deuterium and tritium.

rubric.why: Identifies the three carbon isotopes by their mass numbers.
rubric.how: Award for giving carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 by name or symbol.

rubric.why: Identifies the two common chlorine isotopes by their mass numbers.
rubric.how: Award for giving chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 by name or symbol.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (hydrogen-1, ¹₁H; 1H), deuterium (hydrogen-2, ²₁H; 2H) and tritium (hydrogen-3, ³₁H; 3H).
Carbon has three common isotopes: carbon-12 (¹²₆C; 12C), carbon-13 (¹³₆C; 13C) and carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C; 14C).
Chlorine has two common isotopes: chlorine-35 (³⁵₁₇Cl; 35Cl) and chlorine-37 (³⁷₁₇Cl; 37Cl).

items.followUp: Describe how a coordinate covalent bond forms in the ammonium ion and the hydronium ion.

rubric.why: States the defining feature of a coordinate covalent bond: one atom supplies both shared electrons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that one atom donates both electrons in the shared pair.

rubric.why: Explains that a lone pair is donated to form the bond.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the donated pair as a lone pair and stating that it is donated.

rubric.why: Gives the reactants and product for the ammonium-ion example.
rubric.how: Award for the correct formation of NH4+ from NH3 and H+.

rubric.why: Shows the coordinate bond directed from the nitrogen donor to hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award for showing the N-to-H coordinate bond in the ammonium ion.

rubric.why: Gives the reactants and product for the hydronium-ion example.
rubric.how: Award for the correct formation of H3O+ from H2O and H+.

rubric.why: This point is not used; the question is worth five marks.
rubric.how: Do not award marks for this point.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons of a shared pair to another atom or ion.
The donated pair is usually a lone pair.
In ammonia, nitrogen donates a lone pair to H+: NH3 + H+ → NH4+; the coordinate bond is shown by N→H.
In water, oxygen donates a lone pair to H+: H2O + H+ → H3O+; the coordinate bond is shown by O→H.
The atom donating the lone pair is the donor, and the atom accepting it is the acceptor.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Identifies vapour pressure as pressure associated with vapour above a liquid.
rubric.how: Award for defining vapour pressure as pressure exerted by vapour above its liquid.

rubric.why: Adds the equilibrium condition for the liquid and vapour in a closed container.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the liquid and vapour are in equilibrium in a closed container.

rubric.why: Connects stronger attractions to fewer escaping molecules and lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for stating that stronger intermolecular forces hold molecules in the liquid more tightly and lower vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Connects weaker attractions to more escaping molecules and higher vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for stating that weaker intermolecular forces allow more molecules to escape and raise vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour above its liquid when the vapour and liquid are in equilibrium in a closed container at a given temperature.
Strong intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules more tightly, so fewer escape into the vapour and the vapour pressure is lower.
Weak intermolecular forces allow more molecules to escape into the vapour, so the vapour pressure is higher.

items.followUp: Define solubility and state the general principle that helps predict whether a solute will dissolve in a solvent.

rubric.why: States that solubility concerns the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a solvent.
rubric.how: Award for describing solubility as the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent.

rubric.why: Includes the saturated-solution and temperature conditions in the definition.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the solution is saturated and the temperature is specified.

rubric.why: States the general principle used to predict solubility.
rubric.how: Award for stating that like dissolves like.

rubric.why: Applies the principle to polar and non-polar substances.
rubric.how: Award for matching polar solutes with polar solvents and non-polar solutes with non-polar solvents.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent to form a saturated solution at a specified temperature.
The general principle of solubility is “like dissolves like.”
Polar solutes generally dissolve in polar solvents, while non-polar solutes generally dissolve in non-polar solvents.

items.followUp: Write the names and symbols of any two isotopes of carbon.

rubric.why: Gives the name and symbol or mass-number form of one hydrogen isotope.
rubric.how: Award for naming one hydrogen isotope and giving its correct symbol, such as protium, ¹₁H.

rubric.why: Gives a different hydrogen isotope with its name and symbol or mass-number form.
rubric.how: Award for naming a different hydrogen isotope and giving its correct symbol, such as deuterium, ²₁H, or tritium, ³₁H.

modelAnswer: Protium (hydrogen-1): ¹₁H (1H).
Deuterium (hydrogen-2): ²₁H (2H).

items.followUp: Name one use of uranium-235 in a nuclear power station.

rubric.why: Identifies uranium-235 as fuel for nuclear reactors.
rubric.how: Award for stating that uranium-235 is used as fuel in nuclear reactors.

rubric.why: Identifies its use in nuclear weapons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that uranium-235 is used in atomic bombs or nuclear weapons.

modelAnswer: Uranium-235 is used as fuel in nuclear reactors.
It is also used in atomic bombs.

items.followUp: Why does atomic radius decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Identifies that each successive element down a group has an additional electron shell.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the number of occupied electron shells increases down a group.

rubric.why: Links the additional shells to the greater distance of outer electrons and increased atomic size.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that outer electrons are farther from the nucleus, making the atom larger.

modelAnswer: As we move down a group, each successive element has an additional electron shell.
The outer electrons are therefore farther from the nucleus, so the atomic size increases.
